hero: In a Philippine intensive care unit in Davao City at night, a Filipina nephrology fellow and an ICU nurse prepare a wheeled standard hemodialysis machine with its portable water unit beside a ventilated middle-aged patient, while a male resident studies the bedside monitor showing heart rhythm and blood pressure; cool overhead light, focused teamwork, no text.

figures.teaches: SLED uses the same diffusive circuit as intermittent hemodialysis on a standard machine, run longer and slower so plasma refilling keeps pace with fluid removal.
figures.content: Flat 2D schematic, white background. Modality: SLED (diffusive) - dialysate present, no replacement fluid. Patient at far left with a temporary right internal jugular dual-lumen catheter, tip at the superior vena cava-right atrial junction; one catheter bifurcating into a RED limb (low, level with the arterial line along the bottom) and a BLUE limb (high, level with the venous line along the top), each with a colored terminal cap and clamp, lines joined end to end. Blood path in order along the bottom (red, arrows patient to machine): 'Access pressure (negative, suction)' -> 'Blood pump (roller)' -> 'Pre-filter pressure' inline -> dialyzer BOTTOM END CAP (red, blood inlet). Blood ascends inside the hollow fibers to the TOP END CAP (blue, blood outlet). Along the top (blue, arrows machine to patient): 'Venous pressure' immediately at the dialyzer outlet -> 'Air detector' immediately beside the blue hub, the last component before the patient. Dialyzer side ports carry fluid only: 'Dialysate IN' at the upper side port (teal), running countercurrent DOWN outside the fibers, 'Spent dialysate and ultrafiltrate OUT' at the lower side port (teal) to drain. Small inset cutaway: countercurrent arrows, blood up inside fibers, dialysate down outside. Side box: 'SLED: same machine as intermittent hemodialysis, longer sessions, lower flows; gentler fluid removal'. Footer: '© renalcarematters.com' bottom right, navy. No kidney in the circuit; red and blue for blood only; no replacement fluid line.

figures.teaches: No KRT timing trial found lower mortality with an accelerated start, many delayed patients never needed KRT, and AKIKI 2 marks the limit of waiting.
figures.content: Four horizontal rows, one per trial, each with two bars (early/accelerated vs delayed/standard). Row 1 'AKIKI 2016, 620 patients': day-60 mortality 48.5% vs 49.7%; badge '49% of delayed never received KRT'. Row 2 'IDEAL-ICU 2018, 488 septic shock': day-90 mortality 58% vs 54%; badge '38% of delayed never needed KRT; stopped for futility'. Row 3 'STARRT-AKI 2020, 2,927 analyzed': day-90 mortality 43.9% vs 43.7%; badge 'Dialysis dependence in survivors 10.4% vs 6.0%'. Row 4 'AKIKI 2 2021, 278 already oliguric >72 h or BUN >112 mg/dL': delayed vs more-delayed; 'KRT-free days 12 vs 10'; warning badge 'More-delayed: HR for death 1.65 (secondary analysis)'. Bottom banner: 'Start for urgent indications; otherwise wait with written triggers - but not indefinitely'. Footer: '© renalcarematters.com'.
